common_name: Blue Heaven Little Bluestem (Upright Steel-Blue Native Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Blue Heaven is a sturdy, upright selection of native little bluestem with strong steel-blue summer foliage that turns rich mahogany-orange in fall without flopping open like many wild-type plants.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; little bluestem thrives in poor, rocky, clay, or sandy soil and performs poorly if overfed. Blue Heaven produces strongly upright, steel-blue foliage through summer that transforms into a warm mahogany-orange-red in fall, holding its color and structural form through much of winter, when the fluffy silver seed heads also catch low light beautifully. Its sturdier, more upright habit compared to the straight species resists the flopping that can affect wild little bluestem in rich soil, making it a reliable choice for a naturalistic border or meadow planting. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established and provides valuable habitat and seed for birds; cut back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.

common_name: Standing Ovation Little Bluestem (Extra-Sturdy Non-Flopping Native Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Standing Ovation was bred specifically to solve the late-summer flopping that affects many little bluestem selections in humid, rainy climates, staying upright and tidy all season.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Standing Ovation was specifically selected and trialed for its exceptional stem strength, staying upright through humid, rainy Southern and Midwestern summers where many little bluestem cultivars and the wild species itself tend to splay open or flop by late summer. It carries the same attractive blue-green summer foliage that turns warm orange-copper in fall, along with fluffy silvery seed heads that provide winter interest and bird food. Its reliably upright, dependable form makes it a strong choice for a formal or repeated planting where consistent structure matters, and like other little bluestem selections it is highly drought-tolerant and thrives in poor, lean soil. Cut back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.

common_name: Blackhawks Big Bluestem (Deep Purple-Black Native Prairie Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun; Blackhawks develops unusually deep purple-black foliage color by midsummer, intensifying further into fall, unlike the blue-green typical of the wild species.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun. Blackhawks is a striking big bluestem selection that develops deep, glossy purple-black foliage color as the season progresses, intensifying further with cool fall weather, a dramatic departure from the blue-green summer color of the wild species, topped by the characteristic turkey-foot-shaped seed heads in late summer that give big bluestem its folk name. Like the straight species it is a tall, structural native grass well suited to the back of a border, a naturalized meadow, or a mass planting, tolerating a wide range of soil conditions from moist to fairly dry once established. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges to keep it tidy and vigorous.

common_name: Sioux Blue Indiangrass (Blue-Leaved Native Prairie Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring on well-drained soil in full sun; Sioux Blue is a selection of native indiangrass with notably powdery blue-toned foliage, a cooler color than the yellow-green typical of the wild species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Sioux Blue is a blue-foliaged selection of native indiangrass, a tall prairie grass that produces striking, feathery golden-bronze plumes in late summer above upright, powdery blue-green blades, a cooler and more refined color than the more common yellow-green wild-type indiangrass. It combines well with little and big bluestem in a naturalistic meadow or prairie-style planting, and is highly drought-tolerant and adaptable to a range of soils once established, needing only a late-winter cutback to a few inches before new growth begins. The plumes and seed heads provide winter interest and food for birds if left standing through the dormant season.
